owner_experience.text: The sky roils with eternal anger and lightning yet no rain ever falls. Water is acid, animals are minerals, and life twists under the load… including you.

root_draft.speaker: agent
root_draft.text: The Cauldron is a wet, mineral forest beneath a roiling, rainless storm sky. Its open water carries acid and dissolved poisons, and its fauna carries minerals in living bodies. Its beauty and its livelihood come from chemistry that has reshaped its living things and burdens unprotected newcomers. Cold vents breathe drifting, flammable gas; their falter and the stillness of native animals announce a bloom that loads exposed bodies with metal. Thornwood pays wood and metal for slow, exposed work; mineral creatures turn the same chemistry into food, danger and rare acid-proof plate. The vexxiss tends this breathing ground while fouling water and contesting the colony's taps, and rhossak renew the groves the colony harvests. Roofs, sealed clothing, vexxith and the corroded rigs' filter technology let a colony turn dangerous liquids into useful reagents and drinking water, while acid still threatens unprotected people and ships. Living here means choosing how to work with that ecology, and how much of its burden to take into the colony.

asks.title: What happens to the person who lives here?
asks.picture: Written thought experiment, not a capture or staged game: Two colonists spend weeks working in the Cauldron. One shelters and seals up; the other repeatedly takes the forest's chemistry into their body. They finally leave. The current local mechanics give metal-load illness that fades and acid wounds; I found no Cauldron-specific lasting adaptation.
asks.text: At departure, what should be different about the second colonist, and what in my proposed root misses your meaning of “including you”?
asks.why: F1. Your sentence can mean slow poisoning, a lasting cost, or an actual change in what a person becomes. Those require different core promises; illness alone must not silently stand in for the last one.
asks.guess: I suspect you mean more than an ordinary poison meter, but I would not invent a mutation lottery. My starting guess is a readable, cumulative bodily consequence whose persistence you can describe.
asks.tree_change: If the difference is recoverable illness, bind exposure, noticeable impairment and recovery to the root and add no transformation leaf. If it is lasting damage, require the specific lasting cost and a protected control. If it is adaptation or mutation, add only the change you describe and first resolve its relationship to existing mutation systems; do not build a parallel engine by assumption. A different interpretation rewrites the root. No answer leaves it unapproved.
asks.decision: Meaning of the owner's bodily-consequence promise and correction/approval of expanded root.

asks.title: The first scene that must convince you
asks.picture: Written scene drafts, not staged or accepted: A, a working party reads the vent falter, sees the animals go still, and gets through a bloom. B, a wild vexxiss approaches the colony's tap, drinks and interferes with it while the workers react. C, a colony uses the corroded rig's technology to turn dangerous local fluids into drinking water and useful stock. Each scene includes the forest it belongs in.
asks.text: Which scene would you put first to decide whether this is your Cauldron, and what single wrong moment would make you stop it?
asks.why: F1/F2. The built mod has weather, ecology and industry. I found no owner pick of its flagship demonstration; approving a root would not pick one.
asks.guess: A first: the breathing ground is the common cause of both the life and the industry. Then a different scene for the production loop and another for the giant's interference, with overlap limited to what staging needs.
asks.tree_change: Your selected scene becomes showcase 1 only after your recorded pick; its rejection case supplies the acceptance emphasis. The others remain separate feature scenes or later showcases when they add different coverage. A combined scene also needs independent feature checks and an interaction check. A new scene you describe replaces my candidate list without removing built coverage.
asks.decision: Owner flagship pick, first rejection case and efficient showcase order.

asks.title: A good day after the colony has learned to live here
asks.picture: Written thought experiment, not a staged game: A forty-colonist base has reliable roofs, sealed work clothes, filters, cartridges and ship protection. On a good day its machines work, its workers come home, and it has something useful to show for living here.
asks.text: What still makes that colony plan its day around the Cauldron, and what makes the successful day worth the effort?
asks.why: F3. The individual hazards and machines are already built. Their combined result could be satisfying chemical industry, a continuing negotiation with the wildlife, or repetitive upkeep. The intended successful life is not settled by the current rates.
asks.guess: Competence should buy a workable routine and worthwhile materials. The ecology and an exposed expedition can still change the plan, while correctly used protection remains dependable. I would reject constant busywork as the whole payoff.
asks.tree_change: If successful industry is the payoff, add a sustained production scene with actual supplies, useful output and bounded labour. If the living ecology must remain the central pressure, add the named interruption and a meaningful response alongside that stable baseline. If the successful life is expeditionary, demonstrate what a trip brings home and why staying longer costs more. None of these answers weakens the already-built protection or introduces an unavoidable new tax.
asks.decision: Successful routine, payoff and acceptable ongoing labour at colony scale.

asks.title: A capped vent during a bloom
asks.picture: Written thought experiment, not a staged game: A worker caps a breathing vent. Its gas cloud begins to thin and a tank starts filling. A bloom then arrives. In the current code the cap stops gas emission, but the nearby worker's bloom metal-load calculation still treats that vent as a source; ordinary acidic air is a separate danger.
asks.text: What should the worker be able to infer from that cap, and what should tell you which danger is still present?
asks.why: F2. A cap can truthfully stop a flammable leak while looking like it made the whole area safe. The player must understand what changed before choosing to work beside it.
asks.guess: The sealed leak and the wider weather should have distinct, honest signs. My guess is that capturing the local discharge should reduce its local contribution, while the bloom's wider burden and ordinary acid air still need shelter or gear.
asks.tree_change: If a cap also reduces the local bloom source, bind dose to capping and compare capped/uncapped workers under identical weather, holding other vents and acid exposure fixed. If it controls only the flammable gas, state that boundary and require the remaining bloom danger to be legible. If a cap can cease containing it, define that specific failure and warning before adding any overload mechanic. Existing gas containment and condensate production remain.
asks.decision: Safety meaning of capping and truthful communication of remaining exposure.

asks.picture: Written thought experiment, not a staged game: A wild vexxiss is approaching a working scaffold. It will drink and may damage the scaffold until the vent leaks again. Its tracks can be followed, but the current drinking job can begin prying without an explicit warning about the scaffold.
asks.text: At what moment should you understand what it is about to do, and what useful choice should still be open then?
asks.why: F2/F3. A living rival becomes arbitrary building damage if you discover its purpose after the apparatus fails. The material, drinking and prying mechanics are already there; the missing decision is their readable encounter.
asks.guess: Its approach and interest in the vent should be understandable early enough to withdraw workers, accept the lost production, or protect the equipment. I would start with the creature's readable behaviour and existing tracks rather than assume every arrival needs a letter.
asks.tree_change: If its approach is the warning, require a demonstration where its intent is readable before damage. If a message is necessary, tie it to a real approach/drink state and suppress repeats. If deliberate close work beside it is the accepted risk, bind that shorter response window and make the protected lined-tap contrast explicit. A new response you name gets its own bounded scene; no new taming, wild-shearing or bait system is inferred.
asks.decision: Readable advance cue and usable response in the built wildlife/industry encounter.

asks.title: Burning gas over a pool
asks.picture: Written thought experiment, not a staged game: One continuous cloud lies over a toxic pool and both banks. A spark catches the near bank. The gas can spread over water, but the current burning chain advances through ground fires and creates none on the water, so it can stop before the far bank.
asks.text: What happens above that pool, and what physical boundary should actually stop the burning cloud?
asks.why: F2. Highly flammable gas and ground fire are different things. Choosing the wrong boundary changes whether a pool is protection, whether smoke reaches the far bank, and how the player can contain the hazard.
asks.guess: A continuous flammable cloud can burn over water; the water stops a lasting ground fire, while a real break in gas or a sealed barrier stops the cloud's flame. I would demonstrate that rule beside a genuinely separated cloud.
asks.tree_change: If continuous gas carries ignition across the pool, add a gas-to-gas propagation requirement with a separated-cloud/closed-barrier control and toxic-smoke observations. If the pool reliably stops it, bind that rule and give the player a readable physical explanation. If only dense or short spans carry it, specify the visible condition and test both sides. This does not change the existing requirement that vent gas burns into toxic smoke.
asks.decision: Ignition boundary across water and gas gaps; physical containment rule.

asks.title: A forest after a week of profitable work
asks.picture: Written thought experiment, not a staged game: The colony sends a serious forestry party into mature thornwood over several days. Steel and wood come home; the harvested stand changes. Bound rhossak still sprout the ground, and groups can root new thornwood. Vexxith is a different supply, sheared from a living tame giant on a long cycle.
asks.text: At the end of that week, what should show that the expedition paid, and what price should be visible in the forest and the colony's work?
asks.why: F3. A small metal stack can pass a harvest test without making the biome worth working. Regrowth and grove animals can also erase the cost so quickly that the forest becomes a free resource machine. The right trade-off needs a picture of labour and aftermath.
asks.guess: A worthwhile haul for a real commitment of workers and exposed time, with a visibly worked stand that takes time and living ecology to renew. I would keep the rewards from forestry and living vexxiss distinct rather than make either replace the other.
asks.tree_change: If extraction should visibly deplete old stands, require a before/after work-and-yield scene and a later recovery observation with ordinary growth separated from rhossak effects. If tending groves is the intended sustainable livelihood, require an actual manageable cycle and its labour/material accounting. If forestry is mainly a short visit's windfall, bind that payoff without promising it can sustain a permanent industrial colony. Existing harvesting, binding, sprouting, rooting and shearing stay covered.
asks.decision: Worthwhile forestry labour, ecological cost and recovery at sustained colony scale.

failure_modes: F1: The place tells the wrong story: ordinary daylight or harmless-looking water, plants and animals that read as familiar scenery, or 'including you' reduced to a health number when he meant a changed person. Sources: design/RimMandrake/biome_experiences_2026-10-20.md:9; design/Jawa/worldbuilding/biomes/cauldron.md; OWNER:1792370870264139349.

F2: Its chemistry is arbitrary: a cap looks safe while the worker is dosed, a quiet forest offers no useful warning, fire ignores a believable boundary, or an unannounced giant wrecks the apparatus. Sources: src/RimMandrake/Cauldron/Source/RM_CauldronVents.cs:385; src/RimMandrake/Cauldron/Source/RM_VentGas.cs:210; OWNER:1792108481222070856.

F3: Mastery produces chores or a hollow reward: illness, cartridges and exposed work dominate a large colony without a worthwhile forest/material economy, or isolated tests pass while the study-to-production and ecology loops cannot sustain play. Sources: ITEM:CAULDRON_GPT_ENRICHMENT_1; ITEM:VEXXITH_USES_1; src/RimMandrake/Cauldron/validation.py:2409.
